clue.text: Congratulations, having lofted sixes, almost? (4,5)

blocks.note: lofted = high up in the air
numbers that almost reach sixes

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is pure cricket — batters lofting sixes — but no letters move at all: 'almost sixes' are simply fives, and the question mark owns up to the arithmetic joke.

clue.text: Ferret wounded small creatures in a hole (7)

blocks.note: a hob is a male ferret
past tense of bite
standard abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: Tolkien's opening line — 'In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit' — makes the definition fair. HOB for a male ferret is a crossword staple worth filing away.

clue.text: Try united batter and stew (7)

blocks.note: have a go = have a try
as in Man U
to batter = to lash, as a verb

explanation.walkthrough: The surface wants 'batter' to be the cake mixture next to the stew, but it is the verb — to lash. U for united comes straight off the football results.

clue.text: Social gathering vital for one usually on laptop (8,3)

blocks.note: a function is a formal social event
key = vital, as in 'a key decision'

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is by example: F1 to F12 run along the top of a laptop keyboard, so a function key is 'one usually on laptop'.

clue.text: Selective eaters may have struggles to eat this protein? (7)

blocks.note: vies = struggles, competes
the protein that VIES swallows

explanation.walkthrough: Veggies here are the vegetarians, not the vegetables — the selective eaters. The joke is that the wordplay acts out the surface: VIES really does have to eat an EGG.

clue.text: Had accommodation across river, then wandered off (7)

blocks.note: stayed = had accommodation, as at a hotel
map-key abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: STAYED spans the R just as the surface has the lodgings sitting across the water. R for river is one of the commonest single-letter abbreviations.

clue.text: Tease bird a small distance off (5)

blocks.note: a CHAFFINCH, one of Britain's commonest garden birds, with the INCH removed
the letters taken off the bird

explanation.walkthrough: To chaff someone is to tease them good-naturedly — the banter sense, not the wheat husks the farming-flavoured surface suggests.

clue.text: Agency’s brief goodbye (3)

blocks.note: CIAO, the Italian goodbye, stopped just before the O

explanation.walkthrough: The Central Intelligence Agency, made by cutting a farewell short. In a three-letter entry, 'brief' doing the trimming is nearly always the whole trick.

clue.text: Bail due to be reviewed in hearing (7)

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a courtroom, and 'hearing' completes the legal picture so well that it hides the definition: 'in hearing' — within earshot — is AUDIBLE.

clue.text: Having crossed river, shot by arrow in the head, and left like this? (3,4)

definitions.note: The definition works by completion rather than substitution: someone in the clue's sorry state has been 'left FOR DEAD', so 'left like this?' points at the phrase the answer finishes.

blocks.note: a ford is where you cross a river
HEAD with its top letter shot away — 'EAD

explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry the first letter of HEAD really is its head, and the arrow shoots it off. The whole grisly scene — river forded, arrow in the head — leaves someone for dead.

clue.text: Disaster, going after black bear (5)

blocks.note: as in pencil grades
goes after the B

explanation.walkthrough: Bruin — Dutch for brown — is the bear's name in the medieval Reynard fables, and crosswords have kept it alive ever since.

clue.text: Manipulate voting arrangement, cancelling all-out rally in plant (9)

blocks.note: the base word, before surgery
RALLY with ALL out — and this RY is what gets cancelled

explanation.walkthrough: A deletion built from another deletion: the letters to be removed are themselves manufactured by an earlier removal, which is rare and worth slowing down for. Germander is a family of flowering plants.

clue.text: Princess on stage may sound like a duck (3)

blocks.note: the eider is the sea duck famous for its down

explanation.walkthrough: Princess Ida is Gilbert and Sullivan's operetta — hence 'on stage'. Say IDA aloud and you get 'eider', the duck whose down fills your duvet.

clue.text: Unfortunately still barely functioning as an example (11)

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is self-referential: count the beats in 'func-tion-ing' — three, so the word is itself an example of a trisyllable.

clue.text: Despairing, how ‘miserable’ becomes me (6,5)

blocks.note: to lose heart is to despair
strip the heart — every inner letter — out of MISERABLE and only M…E survives: 'me'

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is an instruction acted out on the word itself: MISERABLE losing its heart leaves just ME. 'Becomes me' adds a layer of false modesty to the gloom.

clue.text: Academy halved deficit in grand house (7)

blocks.note: SCHOOL cut to its first half
a loss = a deficit

explanation.walkthrough: Schloss is the German for a castle or stately home — the grand house. An English academy, halved, opens a German answer.

clue.text: Detectives are liable to exaggerate (7)

blocks.note: Detective Inspectors
'they tend to' = 'they are liable to'

explanation.walkthrough: To distend is to swell or inflate, and blowing something up beyond its true size is exactly what exaggeration does — that shared image is what makes the definition fair.

clue.text: More grim to be nearly naked (7)

blocks.note: informal British slang for stripped bare, one letter longer than the answer with an extra S on the end — drop it

explanation.walkthrough: Stark means bleak, so its comparative answers 'more grim'. STARKERS is gloriously British slang for naked — setters adore it, so file it away.

clue.text: Spy’s simple earring (7)

blocks.note: a long-term undercover agent who lies low for years before being activated
a plain ring worn to keep a new piercing open

explanation.walkthrough: Espionage and jewellery, with nothing in common but the word. Railway sleepers would make it a triple — English works this word hard.

clue.text: Way back, wise guy’s first to drop a board game (4,3)

blocks.note: SAGE'S — a wise guy's — without its opening S
straight from the clue
the ancient Japanese board game

explanation.walkthrough: 'Way back' is the adverb, as in 'way back when'. Note that SAGE keeps its possessive S when its own first letter drops — the apostrophe simply disappears.

clue.text: Turned back, taking opposite directions in circle (7)

blocks.note: east and west, a facing pair on the compass
takes the EW in

explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned back' as a tape or a clock is rewound. Compass points are a setter's favourite way to smuggle in E, W, N and S — 'opposite directions' always means a facing pair.

clue.text: Youngster with Guardian wanting whiskey in pubs shows guts (7)

blocks.note: with the Guardian alongside, this describes a WARD
a youngster with a guardian is a ward — the italics wink at this very newspaper
W in the phonetic alphabet; 'wanting' removes it, leaving ARD
the ARD goes inside

explanation.walkthrough: The italicised Guardian is the setter's wink: a youngster with a guardian is a WARD in the legal sense. Whiskey is the radio operator's W, not the drink the pubs suggest.

clue.text: Happening before delivery to change routine (2,5)

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivery' is the midwife's, not the postman's: in utero means in the womb, so before delivery. A neat single-word anagram — ROUTINE rearranged completely.

clue.text: Run a brief fiddle making pasta (7)

blocks.note: cricket scorecard abbreviation
straight from the clue
VIOLIN — a fiddle — cut short

explanation.walkthrough: Fiddle and violin are the same instrument, one word posher than the other; only the N is lost. The surface's 'brief fiddle' sounds like a minor swindle, which is the misdirection.

clue.text: A way to heave and strain (7)

blocks.note: a street
to retch is to heave, in the queasy sense

explanation.walkthrough: 'Strain' defines STRETCH as verb or noun. The surface implies hauling on a rope, but the heaving here is the stomach's — to retch.

clue.text: Bizarrely we envy almost all that’s horrible in author (6,5)

blocks.note: anagram fodder
ALL stopping short of its last letter
the exclamation of disgust joins the fodder

explanation.walkthrough: Evelyn Waugh wrote Decline and Fall and Brideshead Revisited, and the surface reads like a review of his satire: we do envy almost all that's horrible in him.

clue.text: One checks whistleblower in French department (3)

blocks.note: the Video Assistant Referee reviews the on-pitch referee's decisions
one of the French departments along the Mediterranean coast in Provence, named after the river running through it

explanation.walkthrough: The whistleblower is not a leaker but the referee holding an actual whistle, second-guessed from the VAR booth every football weekend.

clue.text: Wendy’s theatre? (9)

blocks.note: a child's toy Wendy house, named for Wendy in Peter Pan, is a miniature den for pretend games
loads of real theatres use this exact word as their proper name

explanation.walkthrough: The Lost Boys build a little house around Wendy in Peter Pan, which is how toy houses got the name — and since Peter Pan began as a play, the question mark is well earned.

clue.text: Partner dropping by in centre of activity (3)

blocks.note: an informal husband
the letters dropped from HUBBY

explanation.walkthrough: The letters to remove are sitting right there in the clue: hubby drops 'by', and the deletion hides in plain sight as the visitor 'dropping by'.

clue.text: Under way a short distance (5)

blocks.note: an old idiom for something already under way, as in a famous detective's saying
twelve inches make a common unit of length; stick the indefinite article in front of it to build the answer

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer and 'a foot' really is a short distance. 'The game's afoot' was Shakespeare's line in Henry V long before Sherlock Holmes borrowed it.

clue.text: Foreign character doctor found in shape (5)

blocks.note: the Greek letter
Bachelor of Medicine, from the Latin Medicinae Baccalaureus

explanation.walkthrough: A rhomb is a rhombus with its Latin tail docked. Crossword doctors come in many flavours — DR, MO, GP and, as here, MB.

clue.text: Opposite of gauche, that missing husband in spa town (9)

blocks.note: French: gauche is left, droit is right
the pronoun
the abbreviation removed from WHICH

explanation.walkthrough: Droitwich Spa in Worcestershire made its name on salt and brine baths. Droit, the French for right, also gives English 'adroit' — the opposite of gauche in both senses.
